standard.title: Constructing Evidence-Based Arguments
standard.description: construct arguments based on analysis of a variety of evidence to support conclusions or evaluate claims, and consider any ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with accessing, using or citing secondary data or information
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can construct evidence-based arguments and acknowledge ethical issues (AC9S7I07, 7-8 band). They now extend to interrogating secondary source credibility and data validity, evaluating media science claims against their methods, and constructing arguments that acknowledge First Peoples' knowledge contributions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students construct arguments from multiple evaluated evidence sources that support a conclusion or evaluate a claim, and address ethical issues and cultural protocols in the access, use and citation of secondary data — including acknowledgement of First Peoples' knowledge systems.

nodes.label: Secondary evidence is evaluated for credibility and validity before use
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine secondary data for source credibility, data validity and reproducibility, identify multiple consistent sources for a claim, and evaluate whether media science claims are supported by the methods described.
nodes.minimum_width: Students evaluate at least one secondary source for credibility and data validity, and compare it with at least one other source on the same claim.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine secondary data for source credibility, validity and reproducibility; identify multiple consistent sources for a claim (e.g. vaccine effectiveness); interrogate media science reports against the methods used; distinguish between data supporting a claim and data that is consistent with but does not prove it; and recognise when reported findings have been overstated.
wider: Research methods used in studies reported in the media and evaluate the validity of headlines against those methods — examining the gap between what the data shows and how it is reported
Identify multiple consistent sources for a claim such as vaccine effectiveness — examining how convergent independent evidence strengthens the argument
Examine secondary data for personal information risks, correct citation and relevance to the investigation question
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to construct arguments from evaluated evidence. Students who accept secondary sources uncritically cannot build valid arguments — they incorporate data that doesn't support their claim or overlook methodological limitations that undermine the conclusion. Source evaluation in Node 1 is the prerequisite raw material for argument construction in Node 2.

response_modes.reason: Students tend to accept secondary sources uncritically or reject them on superficial grounds (unfamiliar source = untrustworthy). Encountering source evaluation across varied secondary source types — peer-reviewed papers, media reports, government data, industry publications — builds a more principled and transferable credibility assessment capability.

success_criteria: Evaluates at least one secondary source for credibility and data validity with specific reasoning
Identifies whether a media science claim is supported by the methods described in the report

nodes.label: Arguments are constructed from evaluated evidence with ethical and cultural awareness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct an argument from multiple evaluated evidence sources that supports a conclusion or evaluates a claim, and address ethical issues and cultural protocols relevant to the evidence used — including acknowledging First Peoples' knowledge contributions.
nodes.minimum_width: Students construct one argument from at least two evaluated evidence sources with explicit reasoning; acknowledge at least one ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to the evidence used.
nodes.typical_width: Students construct arguments from multiple consistent evidence sources with explicit reasoning chains; acknowledge and identify the relationship between First Peoples' knowledges and contemporary science; construct arguments for First Nations contributions to medicine and health; address cultural protocols in citing or using First Nations knowledge; and evaluate claims about the age of ancient artefacts using multiple evidence types.
wider: Acknowledge and construct an argument for First Nations Australians' contributions to medicine through knowledge of physiological pathways and medicinal delivery systems — examining how two knowledge systems contribute to the same understanding

Interrogate evidence and reasoning used to justify claims about ancient artefact ages — examining how multiple evidence types (radiocarbon dating, stratigraphy, material analysis) combine to build an argument
Examine secondary data to ensure it does not contain personal information that could harm individuals, is correctly cited and is relevant to the investigation question

response_modes.reason: Constructing an argument from evaluated evidence requires students to simultaneously apply source evaluation, evidence selection, logical reasoning, and ethical/cultural awareness — all in a single coherent text. Students who have each as separate skills must now deploy them together. The ethical and cultural dimensions are not add-ons but are integral to the argument's validity and integrity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Peoples' knowledge contribution direction is elaboration-grounded and represents genuine analytical depth — constructing an argument that recognises both knowledge systems requires sophisticated evidence integration and cultural understanding that goes well beyond standard argument-writing.
success_criteria: Constructs an argument from at least two evaluated evidence sources with an explicit reasoning chain connecting evidence to conclusion
Addresses at least one ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to the evidence used — not as a disclaimer but as part of the argument
